extracted.intended_audience: general readers; librarians, educators, and free-speech advocates
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of book banning and challenges in the United States, describing commonly cited reasons for challenges, case examples, policies and advocacy responses. Useful for understanding what content, formats, or circumstances lead to censorship and how institutions respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: ALA top reasons for censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Library Association has observed that the top three reasons for book censorship in the United States are that the material was considered to be 'sexually explicit', the content contained 'offensive language', or the book was 'unsuited to any age group.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the ALA in reporting and tracking challenged and banned books; cited as the most common grounds challengers give when attempting to remove books from libraries or curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office for Intellectual Freedom reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office for Intellectual Freedom cites common reasons for censorship as 'offensive language, racism, unsuited to age group, violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are used to categorize and analyze challenges—examples in the article include Of Mice and Men (racial slurs), Catcher in the Rye (offensive language), and books featuring violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually explicit content
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual content, including explicit descriptions, references to sexual activity, rape, incest, or sexual abuse are frequently cited grounds for challenging or banning books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: To Kill a Mockingbird (discussion of rape), The Perks of Being a Wallflower (references to sexual abuse), Snow Falling on Cedars (compared to pornography). Often listed under 'sexually explicit' by challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive language (including racial slurs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of profanity, vulgar language, or racial slurs is a common reason books are challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Of Mice and Men challenged for racial slurs and 'offensive language'; The Catcher in the Rye challenged primarily for its language. Challenges sometimes seek alternatives that address the same themes without such language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriateness / 'unsuited to any age group'
rubrics_metrics.description: Material deemed inappropriate for the intended readership or 'unsuited to any age group' is a frequent justification for challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges often occur in school settings where parents or boards argue that content is not appropriate for students of a given grade; responses include removing a book from required lists or offering alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial depictions / concerns about racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of race, racial language, or treatment of racial groups (including historical injustices) prompt objections and challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To Kill a Mockingbird faced challenges because a resident objected to how African Americans were treated in the novel; some challengers argue descriptions may upset students of particular backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence and graphic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of violence or graphic scenes are cited as reasons to restrict access to books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed alongside other content-based reasons (sexual content, offensive language); the Office for Intellectual Freedom includes 'violence' as a common reason for challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBTQIA+ content and related objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of LGBTQIA+ characters, themes, or identities can be a stated reason for challenges, sometimes framed as 'creating confusion' or conflicting with religious/traditional family viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alex Gino's Melissa was challenged for 'LGBTQIA+ content' and for 'conflicting with a religious viewpoint' and 'traditional family structure.' Challenges on these grounds have been prominent in recent ALA lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious objections / conflict with religious viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that allegedly conflict with particular religious beliefs or teachings are challenged on the basis that they undermine or contradict religious values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often invoked together with objections about family structure or sexual content; challengers may seek removal from school curricula or library shelves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disrespect to authority / inappropriate humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of characters disrespecting authority or using irreverent humor (especially in children's books) are cited as reasons for banning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Captain Underpants series faced bans for assertions that main characters are disrespectful to authority and that the humor is inappropriate; later efforts increased due to revealing a gay character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/accessibility concerns (illustrations making material accessible to younger children)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of illustrations or an accessible format that may make mature themes reachable to younger children increases the likelihood of challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Fun Home, a graphic novel, faced challenges because illustrations make mature themes more accessible to younger readers; format can change perceived suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum placement decisions versus outright banning
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders may push to remove books from required/mandatory reading lists or recommended curricula rather than demand wholesale banning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Normal, Illinois a group proposed removing Of Mice and Men from the permanent required reading list for sophomores (but did not ask for a ban), and suggested alternative titles addressing the same themes without racial slurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental control and notification policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that give parents more control—such as automatically offering an alternative to a challenged book or notifying parents what books their children read—are used as institutional responses to challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Board voted to require principals to automatically offer an alternative to a challenged book; a district mandated practices to tell parents what books their children read, leaving decisions to parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation measures when retaining contested books
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions may keep a challenged book but implement mitigations (teacher training, sensitivity training) to address community concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A school board voted to keep To Kill a Mockingbird in the curriculum and implemented racial sensitivity training for teachers using the novel as a compromise response to objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/constitutional tests and obscenity standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Court tests for obscenity and First Amendment protections affect whether material is legally bannable—e.g., Miller v. California's three-prong obscenity test and judicial distinctions about 'serious literature or political works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (Kaplan v. California, Miller) and Supreme Court jurisprudence shape the legal threshold for suppression; the Freedom to Read Foundation engages in legal advocacy on these issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: State secrecy / national security and pre-publication censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments or intelligence agencies have suppressed books for reasons of state secrecy, national security, or to prevent disclosure of sensitive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The China Lobby in American Politics was suppressed at the behest of the Chinese Nationalist Party and intervened on by U.S. agencies; CIA-ordered redactions occurred in The CIA and the Cult of Intelligence and were litigated in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy responses and legal support as quality-of-access criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations assess challenges and respond via advocacy, public awareness (Banned Books Week), and legal counsel to protect access to information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Freedom to Read Foundation supplies legal counsel and support; Banned Books Week aims to 'celebrate the freedom to read' and teach the importance of First Amendment rights and the dangers of imposed restraints.
